title: Pointers to Arrays
concept: Array pointers and pointer arrays have different meanings and operation units with a single parenthesis position.

steps.title: Start main function
steps.explanation: The main frame is created and ready for array/pointer comparison.

steps.title: Integer array declaration
steps.explanation:
Stores three integers in contiguous memory in `arr`.

Compare the two types based on this array.

steps.title: Concept 1: Pointers to arrays
steps.explanation:
`int (*p)[3]` is a pointer to "the entire array of size 3".

When performing pointer operations, the unit of movement is the entire size of the array.

steps.title: Concept 2: Array of pointers
steps.explanation:
`int *ptrArr[3]` is an array containing 3 pointers.

Each element can independently point to a different address.

steps.title: Assigning address values ​​to elements of a pointer array
steps.explanation: Connect the actual address to the array element pointer like `ptrArr[0] = &arr[0];`.

steps.title: Array pointer dereference
steps.explanation: Check the array pointer access rules by reading the value of the second element with `*(*p + 1)`.

steps.title: Program exit
steps.explanation:
Exit with `return 0;`.

Bottom line: `int (*p)[N]` and `int *p[N]` are completely different types.

quiz.question: Which of the following correctly declares 'pointer to int array of size 5'?
quiz.explanation:
Without parentheses, it becomes a 'pointer array' containing 5 pointers.
To refer to the entire array, you must enclose it in parentheses like `(*p)`.

misconceptions.wrong: int *p[3] and int (*p)[3] are the same.
misconceptions.correct: The former is an ‘array of pointers’, and the latter is a ‘pointer pointing to an array’.
misconceptions.why: Because of operator precedence, `[]` concatenates before `*`, so the parentheses completely change the meaning.

keyTakeaway: When you want to point to the entire array as one chunk, use the array pointer `TYPE (*NAME)[SIZE]`.
